title: Pólya–Szegő inequality
intro: In mathematical analysis, the Pólya–Szegő inequality (or Szegő inequality) states that the Sobolev energy of a function in a Sobolev space does not increase under symmetric decreasing rearrangement. The inequality is named after the mathematicians George Pólya and Gábor Szegő.

title: Pólya enumeration theorem
intro: The Pólya enumeration theorem, also known as the Redfield–Pólya theorem and Pólya counting, is a theorem in combinatorics that both follows from and ultimately generalizes Burnside's lemma on the number of orbits of a group action on a set. The theorem was first published by J. Howard Redfield in 1927.

title: P/poly
intro: In computational complexity theory, P/poly is a complexity class that can be defined in both circuit complexity and non-uniform complexity. Since the two definitions are equivalent, this concept bridges the two areas.

title: PP (complexity)
intro: In complexity theory, PP, or PPT is the class of decision problems solvable by a probabilistic Turing machine in polynomial time with an error probability of less than 1/2 for all instances. The abbreviation PP refers to probabilistic polynomial time.

title: P (complexity)
intro: In computational complexity theory, P, also known as PTIME or DTIME(nO(1)), is a fundamental complexity class. It contains all decision problems that can be solved by a deterministic Turing machine using a polynomial amount of computation time, or polynomial time.

title: P versus NP problem
intro: The P versus NP problem is a major unsolved problem in theoretical computer science. Informally, it asks whether every decision problem for which a proposed positive answer can be quickly verified can also be quickly solved.

title: Pappus's area theorem
intro: Pappus's area theorem describes the relationship between the areas of three parallelograms attached to three sides of an arbitrary triangle. The theorem, which can also be thought of as a generalization of the Pythagorean theorem, is named after the Greek mathematician Pappus of Alexandria (4th century AD), who discovered it.

title: Pappus's centroid theorem
intro:
In mathematics, Pappus's centroid theorem (also known as  the Guldinus theorem, Pappus–Guldinus theorem or Pappus's theorem) is either of two related theorems dealing with the surface areas and volumes of surfaces and solids of revolution.
The theorems are attributed to Pappus of Alexandria and Paul Guldin.
